Healthcare Analytics

Predicting Billing Amounts and Test Results Using Regression Models

Kelly Adu-Gyamfi

November 14,2025

1 Executive Summary

This analysis examines patient billing patterns and diagnostic test outcomes using classical regression techniques on a synthetic healthcare dataset of 55,500 patient records. Two modeling tasks are addressed:

  • Linear Regression identifying patient characteristics that drive hospital billing amounts.
  • Multinomial Logistic Regression predicting whether a diagnostic test result is Normal, Abnormal, or Inconclusive.

Key findings indicate that medical condition (particularly obesity and diabetes) shows trends toward higher billing, while patient age and admission type significantly influence test result probabilities. Both models have limited predictive power in isolation, but provide actionable direction for healthcare resource planning and clinical decision support.

1.1 Introduction

Healthcare organizations generate extensive data that, when properly analyzed, can reveal patterns in patient outcomes, resource utilization, and operational efficiency. This report applies classical regression modeling to synthetic healthcare data to address two core questions:

  1. Which factors influence hospital billing amounts? (Linear Regression)
  2. Can we predict diagnostic test results? (Multinomial Logistic Regression)

Through statistical modeling and validation, we aim to identify significant predictors and provide actionable insights for healthcare administrators and clinicians.

2 Data Overview

2.1 Source and Characteristics

55,500Patient Records
15Variables
8Categorical
7Numerical
0Missing Values

Data Source: Synthetic dataset generated using Python’s Faker library to resemble real-world healthcare data. Created for statistical modeling practice without violating patient privacy regulations. (kaggle.com/datasets)

2.2 Variable Descriptions

Table 1. Variable descriptions synthetic healthcare dataset.
Variable Type Role Description
Name Categorical ID Patient identifier
Age Numerical Predictor Patient age in years
Gender Categorical Predictor Male / Female
Blood Type Categorical Descriptor Blood group (A+, O−, etc.)
Medical Condition Categorical Predictor Primary diagnosis (Asthma, Cancer, Diabetes, Hypertension, Obesity, Arthritis)
Date of Admission Date Feature Eng. Hospital admission date
Doctor Categorical Descriptor Attending physician name
Hospital Categorical Descriptor Hospital facility name
Insurance Provider Categorical Predictor Insurance company (Aetna, Blue Cross, Cigna, Medicare, UnitedHealthcare)
Billing Amount Numerical Response (Model 1) Total charges billed in USD
Room Number Numerical Descriptor Assigned room number
Admission Type Categorical Predictor Emergency / Elective / Urgent
Discharge Date Date Feature Eng. Date of patient discharge
Medication Categorical Predictor Prescribed medication
Test Results Categorical Response (Model 2) Normal / Abnormal / Inconclusive

3 Problem Statement & Candidate Models

3.1 Model 1 Continuous Response (Linear Regression)

Research Question: Which patient characteristics and admission factors significantly impact the total hospital billing amount?

Analytic Question: Can we predict a patient’s billing amount using Age, Length of Stay, Admission Type, Medical Condition, and Insurance Provider?

\[ \text{Billing Amount}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Age}_i + \beta_2 \text{LengthOfStay}_i + \beta_3 \text{AdmissionType}_i + \beta_4 \text{InsuranceProvider}_i + \beta_5 \text{MedicalCondition}_i + \epsilon_i \]

Model Assumptions:
  • Linearity the response is a linear function of predictors
  • Independence observations are independent of one another
  • Homoscedasticity constant variance of residuals across fitted values
  • Normality residuals are approximately normally distributed
  • No multicollinearity predictors are not highly correlated with each other

3.2 Model 2 Categorical Response (Multinomial Logistic Regression)

Research Question: Can patient characteristics predict whether a diagnostic test result is Normal, Abnormal, or Inconclusive?

Analytic Question: Can we model Test Results using Age, Medical Condition, Medication, and Admission Type?

\[ P(\text{TestResult}_i = k) = \frac{ \exp\!\left(\beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}\,\text{Age}_i + \beta_{2k}\,\text{MedicalCondition}_i + \beta_{3k}\,\text{Medication}_i + \beta_{4k}\,\text{AdmissionType}_i\right) }{ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{3} \exp\!\left(\beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\,\text{Age}_i + \beta_{2j}\,\text{MedicalCondition}_i + \beta_{3j}\,\text{Medication}_i + \beta_{4j}\,\text{AdmissionType}_i\right) } \]

Model Assumptions:
  • Independence of observations
  • No multicollinearity among predictors (VIF < 5)
  • Correct model specification (no omitted variable bias)
  • Sufficient sample size per outcome category

4 Exploratory Data Analysis & Feature Engineering

4.1 Monthly Hospital Admissions Over Time

Rationale: Understanding seasonal trends and overall changes in hospital admissions helps identify periods of high demand and guide resource allocation.

Figure 1. Monthly hospital admissions from 2020–2024. Seasonal patterns and an upward trend are visible.

Interpretation: The line graph shows monthly hospital admissions from 2020 to 2024. Clear seasonal patterns are visible with regular peaks and troughs each year, along with a gradual upward trend. Admissions consistently spike during winter months and dip in summer, while overall peak volumes have grown from ~600 to ~1,000 admissions.

Feature Engineering:

  • Season derived from admission date (Winter / Spring / Summer / Fall) to capture seasonality in models.
  • Admission_Year for yearly trend analysis.
  • Cumulative_Admissions running count for time-series modeling.

4.2 Top 10 Doctors by Patient Count

Rationale: Identifying which doctors see the most patients helps understand workload distribution and potential effects on outcomes.

Figure 2. Top 10 doctors by patient count. Smith-surname physicians dominate the list.

Interpretation: Doctors with the surname “Smith” dominate the top 10, with Michael Smith having the highest patient count. The distribution is right-skewed a few physicians handle a disproportionately large share of patients, raising questions about workload equity and potential outcome differences.

Feature Engineering:

  • High_Patient_Load binary flag (1 = above-average patients, 0 = below).
  • Doctor_Volume_Category Low / Medium / High grouping for modeling.

4.3 Billing Amount by Admission Type and Gender

Rationale: Exploring billing patterns by admission type and gender highlights cost differences that may be predictive for financial or clinical modeling.

Figure 3. Distribution of billing amounts by admission type and gender.

Interpretation: Emergency admissions show both higher median billing and greater variability compared to elective and urgent cases. Minor gender differences appear within admission types, with male patients showing slightly higher median billing in emergency cases. Note: this is a synthetic dataset observed differences may reflect data generation artefacts rather than real clinical patterns.

Feature Engineering:

  • Billing_Category tertile-based grouping (Low / Medium / High).
  • AdmissionGender interaction term combining admission type × gender.

5 Analytical Dataset

Purpose: Before modeling, a clean, feature-engineered analytical dataset was constructed. This involves:

  • Retaining all original variables not requiring transformation.
  • Replacing original variables with feature-engineered versions where appropriate.
  • Standardizing numerical variables for consistent scale.
Table 2. Feature-engineered variables created for predictive modeling.
Variable Type Description
Season Categorical Season of admission derived from Admission_Date (Winter, Spring, Summer, Fall)
Admission_Year Numerical Year extracted from admission date for trend analysis
Cumulative_Admissions Numerical Running cumulative count of admissions over time
High_Patient_Load Binary (0/1) Flag: 1 if doctor sees above-average patients; 0 otherwise
Doctor_Volume_Category Categorical (Low/Med/High) Doctor grouped by patient volume: Low / Medium / High
Billing_Category Categorical (1/2/3) Billing amount categorised by tertiles: Low / Medium / High
AdmissionGender Categorical (Interaction) Interaction term: Admission_Type × Gender
Days_Hospitalized Numerical Length of stay in days: Discharge_Date − Admission_Date

6.1.5 Coefficient Interpretation

The fitted final model is:

\[ \widehat{\text{Billing}} = 25{,}497 + 138\,(\text{Asthma}) - 336\,(\text{Cancer}) + 141\,(\text{Diabetes}) - 0.2\,(\text{Hypertension}) + 309\,(\text{Obesity}) \]

Table 7. Interpretation of stepwise model coefficients.
Condition Coefficient Interpretation Significant
Baseline β₀ = 25,497 Estimated average billing for the reference group Yes
Asthma β₁ = +138 Asthma patients billed ~$138 more than baseline No
Cancer β₂ = −336 Cancer patients billed ~$336 less than baseline No
Diabetes β₃ = +141 Diabetes patients billed ~$141 more than baseline No
Hypertension β₄ ≈ 0 Negligible effect on billing No
Obesity β₅ = +309 Obesity patients billed ~$309 more than baseline Marginal (p=0.139)

6.1.6 Cross-Validation Performance

Table 8. 5-fold cross-validation metrics linear regression.
Metric Value Interpretation
RMSE 14,211 Average prediction error ~$14,211 large relative to mean billing
MAE 12,296 Average absolute error ~$12,296
R-squared (CV) 0.0001 Model explains <0.01% of billing variation in cross-validation
Multiple R-squared 0.00019 Near-zero in-sample fit
Adjusted R-squared 0.0001 Confirms model explains minimal variation after penalizing complexity

Model Limitation: R² ≈ 0.0001 indicates this model performs little better than a naive mean-based estimate. Residuals range from −$27,170 to +$27,267. Medical condition alone is insufficient to predict billing accurately. Richer clinical data (procedure codes, severity scores, length-of-stay) are needed.

6.1.7 Summary & Recommendation

Finding: Medical condition emerged as the most influential predictor of hospital billing, with obesity (+$309) and diabetes (+$141) trending toward higher costs, while cancer (−$336) associated with lower billing. However, the model explains only ~0.02% of billing variation indicating limited predictive power with current predictors.

Recommendation: Supplement with richer clinical data procedure codes, medication dosing, severity metrics, and DRG codes to build meaningful billing prediction models. Focus initial cost containment efforts on obesity and diabetes management programs as the variables showing the strongest directional signals.

6.2.1 Data Sufficiency

Table 9. Dataset sufficiency for multinomial logistic regression.
Criterion Assessment
Sample size 55,500 patients far exceeds requirements for multinomial modeling

Age Continuous numeric usable directly ✓
Medical Condition Multi-level factor dummy-encoded ✓
Medication Categorical factor dummy-encoded ✓
Admission Type 3-level factor dummy-encoded ✓
Missing values No missing values in predictors or response ✓
Multicollinearity VIF < 5 for all predictors no multicollinearity concern ✓

6.2.2 Model Diagnostics

Table 10. Model fit comparison null vs stepwise-selected multinomial model.
Model Residual Deviance AIC Deviance Reduction
Intercept-only (null) 121,944 121,948
Stepwise-selected 60,962.8 60,967.6 60,981.2 (49.9%)

The stepwise-selected model achieves a ~50% reduction in residual deviance relative to the null model, indicating substantial improvement in fit. Both AIC values favor the stepwise model by a wide margin.

6.2.3 Final Model Equations

The stepwise-selected multinomial logistic regression model uses Abnormal as the reference outcome category:

\[ \log \frac{P(\text{Normal})}{P(\text{Abnormal})} = -0.0059 + 0.018\,\text{Age} + 0.235\,I(\text{Urgent}) + 0.027\,I(\text{Obesity}) + \cdots \]

\[ \log \frac{P(\text{Inconclusive})}{P(\text{Abnormal})} = -0.0147 - 0.010\,\text{Age} + 0.120\,I(\text{Urgent}) + 0.015\,I(\text{Obesity}) + \cdots \]

6.2.4 Intercept Coefficients

Table 11. Multinomial intercept coefficients (no predictors). Baseline: Abnormal.
Outcome (vs Abnormal) Intercept Std. Error Baseline Pred. Prob.
Inconclusive vs Abnormal -0.014657 0.010400 ~33%
Normal vs Abnormal -0.005925 0.010377 ~34%

6.2.5 Key Predictor Coefficients & Odds Ratios

Table 12. Key predictor coefficients and odds ratios stepwise multinomial model.
Predictor Outcome vs Abnormal Estimate Std. Error Odds Ratio Dir.
Age Normal vs Abnormal 0.018 0.005 1.018
Age Inconclusive vs Abnormal -0.010 0.004 0.990
Admission: Urgent Normal vs Abnormal 0.235 0.087 1.265
Admission: Urgent Inconclusive vs Abnormal 0.120 0.085 1.127
Condition: Obesity Normal vs Abnormal 0.027 0.012 1.027
Condition: Obesity Inconclusive vs Abnormal 0.015 0.011 1.015

Interpretation of key odds ratios:

  • Age → Normal vs Abnormal (OR = 1.018): Each additional year of age increases the odds of a Normal result by 1.8% relative to Abnormal.
  • Age → Inconclusive vs Abnormal (OR = 0.990): Each additional year decreases the odds of Inconclusive by 1%.
  • Urgent Admission → Normal vs Abnormal (OR = 1.265): Urgently admitted patients have 26.5% higher odds of a Normal result than the reference admission type.
  • Obesity → Normal vs Abnormal (OR = 1.027): Obesity patients have 2.7% higher odds of a Normal result a small but consistent signal.

6.2.6 Cross-Validation Performance

Table 13. 5-fold cross-validation metrics multinomial logistic regression.
Metric Value Interpretation
Overall Accuracy 0.342 Marginally above the no-information rate
No-Information Rate 0.336 Accuracy of always predicting the majority class
Kappa 0.0116 Near-zero agreement beyond chance
Sensitivity Normal 0.33 Detects 33% of true Normal cases
Sensitivity - Abnormal 0.57 Detects 57% of true Abnormal cases best-performing class
Sensitivity - Inconclusive 0.12 Detects only 12% of Inconclusive cases worst-performing class
Specificity - Normal 0.68 Correctly excludes 68% of non-Normal cases
Specificity - Abnormal 0.44 Correctly excludes 44% of non-Abnormal cases
Specificity - Inconclusive 0.88 Correctly excludes 88% of non-Inconclusive cases

6.2.7 Summary & Recommendation

Finding: Patient age, admission type, and medical condition influence the probability of Normal, Abnormal, and Inconclusive test results. Abnormal results are detected most reliably (sensitivity = 0.57), while Inconclusive results remain difficult to predict (sensitivity = 0.12).

Application: The model can support clinical decision-making by flagging patients at elevated risk of inconclusive results for early follow-up testing.

Recommendation: Incorporate additional clinical predictors lab values, vital signs, comorbidity counts to improve Inconclusive detection. Consider a two-stage model: first classify Abnormal vs Non-Abnormal, then distinguish Normal from Inconclusive within the Non-Abnormal group.

7.1 Future Research Directions

  1. Richer predictors for billing: Procedure codes, DRG classification, medication costs, ICU vs. general ward, surgeon identity.
  2. Non-linear modeling: Gradient boosting or random forests may capture non-linear billing patterns better than OLS regression.
  3. Inconclusive test prediction: Two-stage classification or cost-sensitive learning to improve detection of the hardest outcome class.
  4. Temporal modeling: Time-series or panel methods to exploit the longitudinal structure of the admission data (2020–2024).
  5. Causal inference: Matching or instrumental variable methods to move beyond association toward actionable causal estimates of intervention effects.
